note: Second-pass CRE Set 3 items. Not copied from Set 2. Each display equation is on its own line.

questions.stem:
A constant failure rate is given as a percent per 1,000 hours. That statement means 0.05 failures per unit per 1,000 hours.
\[
\lambda=\frac{0.05}{1000}
\]
\[
MTTF=\frac{1}{\lambda}
\]
What is the MTTF?
questions.why: Convert the percent to a count, divide by 1,000 hours, and invert. \[ \lambda=0.00005 \] \[ MTTF=\frac{1}{0.00005}=20000 \] 200 hours treats the 5 as a count of failures rather than 5 percent. 1,000 hours is the time base. 50,000 hours uses 2 percent instead of 5 percent. B. 20,000 hours

chart.title: Failure rate statement
chart.altText: The constant failure rate is 5 percent per 1,000 hours.

questions.stem:
In one life-table interval, \(d\) units fail out of \(n\) units that entered the interval. The interval width is \(\Delta t\).
\[
h=\frac{d}{n\Delta t}
\]
What is the interval hazard rate?
questions.why: Divide the failures by the number entering, then divide by the interval width. \[ d/n=10/200=0.05 \] \[ h=0.05/100=0.0005 \] 0.0500 is the conditional probability of failure in the interval, not a rate per hour. 0.0050 divides by 10 hours. 10 is the failure count. B. 0.0005 per hour

traps.A: Stops at the conditional failure probability.

chart.title: Life-table interval
chart.altText: Two hundred units entered the interval. Ten failed. The interval is 100 hours wide.

questions.stem:
A normal strength distribution has both tails outside the specification. The tail probabilities are given.
\[
p=p_L+p_U
\]
What fraction of units is nonconforming?
questions.why: Add the two tails. The conforming fraction is not the nonconforming fraction. \[ p=0.0228+0.0062=0.0290 \] 0.0062 and 0.0228 are single tails. 0.9710 is the fraction inside the limits. C. 0.0290

chart.title: Specification tails
chart.altText: The lower-tail probability is 0.0228. The upper-tail probability is 0.0062.

questions.stem:
The sample size for a proportion uses the stated normal factor \(z\), the planning proportion \(p\), and the margin \(E\).
\[
n=\frac{z^{2}p(1-p)}{E^{2}}
\]
What sample size does the formula give?
questions.why: Square the factor, multiply by \(p(1-p)\), and divide by the squared margin. \[ z^{2}p(1-p)=4(0.25)=1 \] \[ n=1/(0.10)^{2}=100 \] 400 omits \(p(1-p)\). 25 stops before dividing by \(E^{2}\). 10 divides \(z\) by \(E\). B. 100

traps.D: Divides the factor by the margin.

chart.title: Proportion sample size
chart.altText: The normal factor z is 2. The planning proportion is 0.50. The margin E is 0.10.

questions.stem:
One unit operates. Two identical units are in cold standby, the switches are perfect, and a standby unit does not fail while waiting. Use \(e^{-1}=0.3679\). At the mission age, \(\lambda t=1\).
\[
R=e^{-\lambda t}\left(1+\lambda t+\frac{(\lambda t)^{2}}{2}\right)
\]
What is the mission reliability, to four decimal places?
questions.why: Two spares add the squared term. One spare stops at \(1+\lambda t\). \[ 1+1+1/2=2.5 \] \[ R=0.3679(2.5)=0.9198 \] 0.7358 is the reliability with one spare. 0.3679 is the operating unit alone. 0.0802 is one minus the two-spare reliability. A. 0.9198

chart.title: Two cold spares
chart.altText: Lambda t is 1. Both spares are cold, and both switches are perfect.

questions.stem:
The top event occurs only if three independent basic events occur. Their probabilities are \(q_1\), \(q_2\), and \(q_3\).
\[
Q=q_1 q_2 q_3
\]
What is the top-event probability?
questions.why: An AND gate multiplies independent event probabilities. \[ Q=(0.05)(0.04)(0.50)=0.001 \] 0.350 adds the three probabilities. 0.050 is the largest input. 0.999 subtracts that input from 1. C. 0.001

chart.title: AND gate
chart.altText: Three independent basic events have probabilities 0.05, 0.04, and 0.50. All three must occur.

questions.stem:
A dangerous failure rate is \(\lambda_D\). Diagnostic coverage \(DC\) is the fraction of those failures that the diagnostics detect. The undetected dangerous rate is
\[
\lambda_{DU}=\lambda_D(1-DC)
\]
What is \(\lambda_{DU}\)?
questions.why: Coverage removes the detected fraction. The undetected fraction is \(1-DC\). \[ 1-DC=0.10 \] \[ \lambda_{DU}=0.001(0.10)=0.0001 \] 0.0009 is the detected portion. 0.0010 ignores the diagnostics. 0.9000 is the coverage, not a rate. D. 0.0001 per hour

traps.A: Multiplies by the coverage instead of by one minus the coverage.

chart.title: Diagnostic coverage
chart.altText: The dangerous failure rate is 0.001 per hour. The diagnostics detect 90 percent of those failures.

questions.stem:
A device is rated \(P_{rated}\) at the base temperature. Above that temperature, the allowable power falls by the stated slope. The application is at the temperature in the table.
\[
P_{allow}=P_{rated}-s\Delta T
\]
Which conclusion follows?
options: Acceptable. The applied power is below the 2.00 W rating.
Acceptable. The derating removes only 0.50 W.
Not acceptable. The derated limit is 1.50 W, and 1.80 W is above it.
Not acceptable. Any temperature above 70 degrees C is forbidden.
questions.why: Subtract the temperature penalty from the rating, then compare the application with that limit. \[ \Delta T=95-70=25 \] \[ P_{allow}=2.00-0.02(25)=1.50 \] The applied 1.80 W is below the nameplate rating and above the derated limit. The slope is a reduction, not a ban on every higher temperature. C. Not acceptable. The derated limit is 1.50 W, and 1.80 W is above it.

traps.A: Compares the application with the nameplate rating.
traps.B: Treats the reduction as proof that the application is acceptable.
traps.D: Turns a slope into a hard temperature ban.

chart.title: Power derating
chart.altText: The device is rated 2.00 W at 70 degrees C. Above 70 degrees C the allowable power falls by 0.02 W per degree C. The application is 1.80 W at 95 degrees C.

questions.stem:
Three suppliers ship the shares below. A unit comes from one supplier at random. The supplier reliabilities are \(R_i\).
\[
R=p_1 R_1+p_2 R_2+p_3 R_3
\]
What is the reliability of a randomly received unit?
questions.why: Weight each supplier by its share of the shipments. \[ R=0.50(0.98)+0.30(0.90)+0.20(0.80) \] \[ R=0.490+0.270+0.160=0.920 \] 0.980 is the best supplier. 0.800 is the worst. 0.893 averages the three reliabilities and ignores the shares. B. 0.920

chart.title: Supplier mix
chart.altText: Supplier A ships half of the units at reliability 0.98. Supplier B ships 30 percent at reliability 0.90. Supplier C ships 20 percent at reliability 0.80.

questions.stem:
The reorder point covers expected demand during the lead time plus the stated safety stock. Weekly demand is \(d\), lead time is \(L\) weeks, and safety stock is \(S\).
\[
ROP=dL+S
\]
What is the reorder point?
questions.why: Multiply the weekly demand by the lead time, then add the safety stock. \[ dL=6(2)=12 \] \[ ROP=12+4=16 \] 12 units omits the safety stock. 6 units is one week of demand. 4 units is only the safety stock. A. 16 units

traps.B: Covers the lead time and omits the safety stock.

chart.title: Spare reorder point
chart.altText: Demand is 6 units per week. The replenishment lead time is 2 weeks. Safety stock is 4 units.
